requirements.text: Respect the global/per-URL toggle: if content blocking is disabled for the current first-party URL, a request must not be blocked.
requirements.findings:
Both blocking backends implement the toggle as an early-return short-circuit inside their respective `_is_blocked()` methods, verified by direct read.

hostblock.py line 114 — `_is_blocked(self, request_url, first_party_url=None)`:
  • Line 116–117: `if not self.enabled: return False` (module-level guard).
  • Lines 119–120: if `first_party_url` is present but invalid it is normalised to `None`.
  • Line 124–125: `if not config.get("content.blocking.enabled", url=first_party_url): return False` — the toggle check. Passes `first_party_url` (possibly `None` after normalisation) as the URL context for per-site config resolution.
  • The set-membership check (lines 128–130) is only reached when the toggle is True.

braveadblock.py line 136 — `_is_blocked(self, request_url, first_party_url=None, resource_type=None)`:
  • Line 143–146: `if not self.enabled: return False` (module-level guard).
  • Lines 148–157: if `first_party_url` is None, invalid, or a file-scheme URL, returns False immediately (no blocking, no config check).
  • Line 161–163: `if not config.get("content.blocking.enabled", url=first_party_url): return False` — the toggle check. Only reached when `first_party_url` is a valid, non-file URL.
  • The engine call (`self._engine.check_network_urls(...)`, line 165) is only reached when the toggle is True.

In both backends, disabling `content.blocking.enabled` (globally or per-site) prevents any blocklist lookup from occurring.

requirements.text: Respect whitelist overrides first: if a request URL matches a whitelist rule, it must not be blocked regardless of any host or parent-domain matches.
requirements.findings:
Neither `hostblock.py` nor `braveadblock.py` applies the whitelist check as an early, first-class guard.

**hostblock.py (lines 128-130):**
The return expression is:
  `return (host in self._blocked_hosts or host in self._config_blocked_hosts) and not blockutils.is_whitelisted_url(request_url)`
The whitelist check (`is_whitelisted_url`) is the trailing `and not` operand. Python short-circuit evaluation means it is only called if a blocklist match is found first — the whitelist is structurally subordinate to the blocklist check, not an upfront override. For the current host-exact matching, all four input combinations (whitelisted×blocked) produce identical return values under either ordering, so there is no observable output difference today. The structural violation becomes a behavioral defect once a subdomain-widening loop is introduced (req-003/req-004): a trailing `and not` expression cannot safely wrap a multi-iteration loop; an early `if blockutils.is_whitelisted_url(request_url): return False` guard preceding the loop is required.

**braveadblock.py (lines 165-193):**
The engine call (`self._engine.check_network_urls(...)`) runs at line 165 unconditionally. The `is_whitelisted_url` check appears at line 187, reached only after the negative guard `if not result.matched: return False` at line 171 and the exception-rule check at line 173. If the engine reports no match, the whitelist is never consulted. The requirement demands whitelist be respected first, independently of any engine result. Note: the return value is False in either ordering for all input combinations, but the structural position violates the "whitelist first" requirement. One minor side-effect difference exists: when a URL is both engine-matched, exception-covered, AND whitelisted, the current path fires a `logger.debug(...)` call at lines 180-185 before returning False; an early whitelist guard would bypass that log entirely.

**`blockutils.is_whitelisted_url` (lines 159-162):**
`return any(pattern.matches(url) for pattern in whitelist)` — checks `config.val.content.blocking.whitelist`. The function itself is correct; the defect is where and when it is called in each backend.

requirements.text: Treat a blocked registrable domain as covering all of its subdomains: if example.com is blocked, then example.com, sub.example.com, and a.b.example.com must all be blocked unless explicitly whitelisted.
requirements.findings:
The requirement demands that blocking example.com also blocks sub.example.com and a.b.example.com. Neither backend implements this.

**hostblock.py (lines 127-130):**
`_is_blocked` extracts the single exact hostname from the request URL and performs two bare set-membership tests:

```python
host = request_url.host()
return (
    host in self._blocked_hosts or host in self._config_blocked_hosts
) and not blockutils.is_whitelisted_url(request_url)
```

There is no loop, no label-stripping, and no parent-domain widening. A request to `sub.example.com` produces `host = "sub.example.com"`, which is checked literally — it will not match a blocklist entry of `"example.com"`. The requirement is structurally impossible to satisfy as written.

**braveadblock.py (lines 165-193):**
The Python layer delegates entirely to `self._engine.check_network_urls(...)`. Whether subdomains are blocked depends solely on whether the upstream filter rules are written as network-level patterns (e.g., `||example.com^`). The Python code contains no explicit subdomain-widening logic of its own; it is transparent to the engine's interpretation.

**_widened_hostnames (configutils.py:42-48):**
A correctly-implemented widening generator (`a.c.foo → [a.c.foo, c.foo, foo]`) already exists, but its only call-site is `configutils.py:234`, inside the per-URL config resolution system (used to resolve scoped config values like per-site settings). It is never imported or invoked from `hostblock.py` or `braveadblock.py`. The function needed to fix req-003 exists in the config layer but is disconnected from the blocking path.

requirements.text: Determine blocking by checking the request host and each successive parent domain (left-stripping one label at a time) against both the runtime blocked set and the config-defined blocked set; the first match blocks the request.
requirements.findings:
req-004 requires an iterative widening loop: for each candidate hostname derived by successively stripping the leftmost label, check it against BOTH the runtime blocked set (`_blocked_hosts`) AND the config-defined set (`_config_blocked_hosts`), returning True on the very first match.

The current implementation in `hostblock.py:_is_blocked` does none of this:

```python
host = request_url.host()          # single exact extraction
return (
    host in self._blocked_hosts or host in self._config_blocked_hosts
) and not blockutils.is_whitelisted_url(request_url)
```

There is no loop, no label-stripping, and no parent-domain widening. Only the single exact hostname extracted at line 127 is tested. A request to `sub.example.com` produces `host = "sub.example.com"` which is then tested literally — it will never match a blocklist entry of `"example.com"`. The "first match blocks" semantic is entirely absent because the two set-membership tests are part of a single Python `or` expression on the same value, not a loop over widened candidates.

The `_widened_hostnames` generator in `configutils.py:42-48` correctly implements the required left-label-stripping iteration (`a.c.foo → [a.c.foo, c.foo, foo]`) and is used at `configutils.py:234` for per-URL config scoping. However, a Grep search confirms it is never imported or called anywhere in `hostblock.py`. The mechanism needed to satisfy req-004 exists in the codebase but is entirely disconnected from the blocking path.

requirements.text: Work with full URLs (including scheme): a request like https://blocked.example.com/... must be evaluated based on its host and handled consistently with plain host strings.
requirements.findings:
Both backends correctly decompose a full URL into its host component before performing any blocklist comparison, satisfying the requirement that a request like `https://blocked.example.com/path` is evaluated based solely on its host.

**hostblock.py (`_is_blocked`, lines 122–130):**
`request_url` arrives as a `QUrl` — Qt's URL type that carries the full request URL, including scheme, host, path, and query. At line 127:
```python
host = request_url.host()
```
`QUrl.host()` extracts only the hostname component, stripping the scheme, port, path, query, and fragment entirely. That string is then compared against `_blocked_hosts` and `_config_blocked_hosts` on line 129:
```python
host in self._blocked_hosts or host in self._config_blocked_hosts
```
The types align: full URL → `QUrl.host()` → bare hostname → set membership test against stored bare hostnames. There is no code path where the presence of a scheme could cause a mismatch.

**braveadblock.py (`_is_blocked`, lines 165–169):**
```python
result = self._engine.check_network_urls(
    request_url.toString(),
    first_party_url.toString(),
    _resource_type_to_string(resource_type),
)
```
The adblock engine receives the full URL string and parses it natively. Filter engines of this type require full URLs so they can inspect scheme, host, and path for network-level rules. Passing `toString()` here is correct and intentional — the engine handles URL decomposition internally.

**blockutils.is_whitelisted_url (lines 159–162):**
```python
def is_whitelisted_url(url: QUrl) -> bool:
    whitelist = config.val.content.blocking.whitelist
    return any(pattern.matches(url) for pattern in whitelist)
```
Receives the full `QUrl` and matches against URL patterns in `content.blocking.whitelist`. Pattern matching operates on complete URLs, so scheme presence is handled naturally.

**Summary:** `QUrl.host()` at hostblock.py:127 is the single point of URL-to-hostname conversion, correctly handling any scheme by stripping all non-host parts. The requirement is fully satisfied as-is.

requirements.text: Handle hosts with trailing dots equivalently to their non-trailing forms during domain matching (e.g., example.com. should behave like example.com).
requirements.findings:
hostblock.py:_is_blocked does not strip a trailing dot from the hostname before performing blocklist lookups. At line 127, `host = request_url.host()` is used verbatim. If the request URL carries a trailing dot (e.g. `http://example.com./path`), Qt's `QUrl.host()` returns `"example.com."`, which fails to match the stored blocklist entry `"example.com"` — the request goes unblocked (set membership test at line 129 returns False).

By contrast, `configutils.py:234` explicitly applies `.rstrip('.')` with the comment: "Urls trailing with '.' are equivalent to non-trailing types. urlutils strips them, so in order to match we will need to as well." That established pattern is entirely absent from `hostblock.py`.

`braveadblock.py` passes the full URL string to the upstream adblock engine via `request_url.toString()` at line 166; trailing-dot handling there is engine-internal and not verified at the Python layer, but no Python-side strip is applied either.

requirements.text:
Define hostname widening semantics:

- For a multi-label hostname like a.b.c, the widening sequence is ["a.b.c", "b.c", "c"].

- For a single-label hostname like foobarbaz, the sequence is ["foobarbaz"].

- For an empty string, the sequence is empty.

- Edge forms must be preserved/processed as strings: ".c" should yield [".c", "c"]; "c." should yield ["c."]; ".c." should yield [".c.", "c."].
requirements.findings:
All six cases specified in req-007 are fully and correctly implemented by the existing private function `_widened_hostnames` in `configutils.py:42-48`.

The algorithm uses `str.partition(".")[-1]` as the left-label stripping step inside a `while hostname:` loop:

1. Multi-label `a.b.c`: yields "a.b.c", then "b.c", then "c"; stops when `partition(".")[-1]` returns "" → `["a.b.c","b.c","c"]` ✓
2. Single-label `foobarbaz`: `partition(".")` returns `("foobarbaz","","")`, so `[-1]=""` is falsy after one yield → `["foobarbaz"]` ✓
3. Empty string `""`: `while hostname:` is immediately False, no yields → `[]` ✓
4. `.c`: first `partition(".")` gives `("",".","c")` so `[-1]="c"` (truthy), second gives "" → `[".c","c"]` ✓
5. `c.`: `partition(".")` gives `("c",".","")` so `[-1]=""` falsy after one yield → `["c."]` ✓
6. `.c.`: first `partition(".")` gives `("",".",".c.")` so `[-1]="c."` (truthy), second gives `("c",".","")` → `[".c.","c."]` ✓

The test class `TestWiden` at `test_configutils.py:305-315` explicitly asserts every one of these cases. The semantics are therefore already defined, implemented, and test-verified in the codebase. The only gap relevant to the broader repair is that this function is private (`_widened_hostnames`) and lives in `configutils.py` rather than in `urlutils.py` as a public export — but that is the concern of req-008, not req-007. Req-007 purely defines the widening semantics, and those are AS_IS_COMPLIANT.

requirements.text:
Name: widened_hostnames
Input: hostname: str 
Output: Iterable[str] 
Description: Generates parent-domain variants of a hostname by successively removing the leftmost label.
Pathfile: qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.py
requirements.findings:
The public function `widened_hostnames(hostname: str) -> Iterable[str]` does not exist anywhere in `qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.py`. A grep search for `widened_hostnames` across the entire codebase found zero matches in urlutils.py, and a scan of all `def` statements in urlutils.py confirms 24 definitions — none named `widened_hostnames`.

A semantically equivalent private function `_widened_hostnames` exists at `qutebrowser/config/configutils.py:42-48`, confirmed by direct Read:

    def _widened_hostnames(hostname: str) -> Iterable[str]:
        """A generator for widening string hostnames.
        Ex: a.c.foo -> [a.c.foo, c.foo, foo]"""
        while hostname:
            yield hostname
            hostname = hostname.partition(".")[-1]

However it is:
- Private (underscore-prefixed).
- Located in `configutils.py`, not `urlutils.py`.
- Only called at one internal site (`configutils.py:234`): `widened_hosts = _widened_hostnames(url.host().rstrip('.'))`.
- Never imported or re-exported from `urlutils.py`.

The requirement demands a public function named `widened_hostnames` residing in `qutebrowser/utils/urlutils.py`. That definition is entirely absent — the function must be created (or moved/re-exported) there.
